card.hook: Picture an emperor leaning out of a balcony, drink in hand, watching a tournament in the square below. That's the Golden Roof, and you get to see it with ice cream instead of armour.
card.stand_here: Stand on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße, mid-street, with the Golden Roof about 16 m ahead, to the north. Face north and you'll get the roof in the centre of the frame, with pastel Old Town buildings on both sides and the Nordkette mountains rising behind the rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the narrow street, the roof and the mountains all in one go. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved reliefs and coats of arms on the balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the golden roof, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the gold keeps its detail and the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The street is calmer and the light is kinder than the harsh midday sun, when the pedestrian zone gets very busy.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the open square directly in front of the Golden Roof, on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße, with the gilded front behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt it up so the roof sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back mid-street on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße so the whole balcony and roof fit in the shot, while you pose in front of the roof; a slightly off-centre angle works better when it's busy.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside of the Golden Roof from the open pedestrian street at any time, but the balcony can only be seen from inside the museum, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take your wide street shot first, then zoom in and find one coat of arms on the balcony. Bonus points for a second frame that sneaks in the richly decorated Helblinghaus.
card.good_to_know: The Golden Roof was finished in 1500 for Emperor Maximilian I, who wanted a private box where he and his wife, Bianca Maria Sforza, could watch festivals and tournaments in the square. It carries about 2,657 fire-gilded copper tiles, though other counts say 2,738. The carved reliefs and painted panels you see today are careful replicas, and the originals are kept in the Ferdinandeum museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße, mid-street, with the Golden Roof about 16 m ahead, to the north. Face north and you'll get the roof in the centre of the frame, with pastel Old Town buildings on both sides and the Nordkette mountains rising behind the rooftops.

card.hook: Picture a row of candy-coloured houses lined up along the river, with a huge wall of grey rock looming right behind them. That's Innsbruck's famous city-and-mountain shot, and you get it from one square.
card.stand_here: Stand in Marktplatz, a short walk from the Golden Roof. Face north across the Inn towards the Mariahilf houses, with the Nordkette ridge rising behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the river, the houses and the ridge all fit in one frame. If the mountain looks small, try zoom 2x to make it feel bigger behind the houses.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the row of houses on the lower third, and keep your phone level so the houses don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun is behind you and lights up the houses (one guide recommends this). Check the forecast first, because the peaks are often hidden in cloud.
card.selfie_here: Head to Herzog-Friedrich-Straße and stand mid-street in front of the Golden Roof, so it's centred with the Nordkette rising behind you. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, to squeeze in the roof and the mountain over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Along the north edge of the Hofgarten, where the Nordkette shows past the trees, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the ridge behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Alpine weather changes quickly and can turn snowy or icy outside peak summer, so if you hike beyond the cable car stations, go properly equipped. The cable cars and the Bergisel ski-jump tower are separate and may be ticketed, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Catch all three layers in one frame: water, bright façades, then rock. Bonus points if the clouds clear just for you.
card.good_to_know: The Nordkette is the steep ridge that rises straight up behind Innsbruck, and it's what makes the city look so dramatic. Several guides call this the classic city-and-mountain shot. If the top is in cloud, the houses and river still make a pleasant photo, just without the mountain as the star.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Marktplatz, a short walk from the Golden Roof. Face north across the Inn towards the Mariahilf houses, with the Nordkette ridge rising behind them.

card.hook: Picture a castle built as a gift for a wife, then stuffed with its owner's collections. That's Ambras, up in the hills above Innsbruck, and its courtyard is where the good photos are.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in Unterschloss, the lower castle courtyard inside the grounds. Face the castle's Renaissance buildings so the old walls, arcades and formal gardens fill the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the courtyard and castle together. If it feels tight, tap 0.5x to fit in the arcades and gardens, and use 2x or more (depends on your phone) for details on the facades.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up an arcade or building edge with a vertical line so the walls stay straight, with a strip of garden at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: One guide recommends midday light for this courtyard. If you want a second shot with Innsbruck and the mountains, the Belvedere works well at sunset.
card.selfie_here: Try the inner courtyard under the arcades, beside the Renaissance fountain. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the arches and fountain over your shoulder. Early morning is quieter, so you'll have fewer people in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little way down the approach drive that climbs to the castle, while you stand higher up with the castle behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are generally fine in most areas of the castle collections, but check for signs inside the exhibits. Ambras is a museum with grounds, so it may be ticketed or have seasonal restrictions. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the corner where an arch frames the castle best, then take the same shot from the next corner and see which one you'd put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: Ambras sits 632 metres above sea level, and the 16th-century castle was built on the site of a 10th-century one. Archduke Ferdinand II had it rebuilt as a gift for his wife, Philippine Welser. He built the Lower Castle specially for his collections, which makes this one of the oldest museums in the world.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in Unterschloss, the lower castle courtyard inside the grounds. Face the castle's Renaissance buildings so the old walls, arcades and formal gardens fill the frame.

card.hook: Most ski jumps look like a ramp. This one looks like a sleek swoosh sketched across the Innsbruck skyline, and that long, tapering line is made for a phone photo.
card.stand_here: Head for the Bergisel Ski Jump (Bergiselschanze), where the phone icon on the map sits right at the jump. Then face the jump and walk back as far as you safely and legally can, so the whole shape fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole jump in, then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view. Try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for a close shot of one detail of the structure.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the long diagonal of the jump through the picture, keeping your phone level so the vertical parts don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters a structure like this, and a clear day gives you a clean sky behind it. Competition days are busier, so allow extra time.
card.selfie_here: Go up to the outdoor viewing platform at the top of the tower (Bergisel Sky), which visitors call a great selfie spot. Use the front camera, hold it a little above eye level, and get the city and mountains behind you.
card.ask_someone: Try the spectator stands below the jump: hand your phone to a passer-by, ask them to step back, and stand with the jump behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on public paths and in areas you're allowed in, and follow any signs or staff instructions. Check the official site for access details before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three different distances, then pick the one where the jump looks most dramatic, ideally with a person in the foreground to show how big it is.
card.good_to_know: The stadium has room for 26,000 people, and the jump hosts the third competition of the Four Hills Tournament every year. The first competitions here in the 1920s used simple wooden constructions, and a larger hill followed in 1930. It was rebuilt before the 1964 Winter Olympics, used again in 1976, and the hill you see today was finished in 2003, designed by Zaha Hadid.

card.hook: The Hofburg's long, calm front is a gift to a phone camera: clean Baroque lines, soft colours, and a tower hiding a past as a city gate. The only thing that gets in the way is the occasional bus.
card.stand_here: Stand near Rennweg, about 25 m north-east of the Hofburg, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You're very close, so the palace will fill most of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If you can't step back far enough, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a tower, a doorway or a row of windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the façade with a vertical line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day in the morning or late afternoon, when the softer light gives the façade more shape. Mornings usually mean fewer people in your shot too.
card.selfie_here: Try the inner courtyard, with the white façade behind you and the Alps showing above the roofline. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to fit more of the palace in, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are not allowed inside the museum and imperial rooms, phones included, so keep your camera for the outside. The courtyard pick comes from a single guide, so check it's open when you arrive.
card.challenge: Take the same wall twice, once wide and once zoomed in on one tiny detail, and see which one you'd put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: The first palace was built around 1460 under Archduke Sigismund. The main façade on the Rennweg dates from 1766 to 1773, in the time of Empress Maria Theresa. Look for the Heraldic Tower, converted in 1499 from an earlier city gate. The palace stayed with the Habsburgs for more than 450 years and today holds museum rooms, so check the official site for access and ticket rules.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Rennweg, about 25 m north-east of the Hofburg, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You're very close, so the palace will fill most of your screen.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: the grand black marble tomb in the middle of this church is empty, and 28 bronze figures, each taller than you, stand guard around it anyway.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Court Church (Hofkirche) at Universitätsstraße 2, next to the Hofburg, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Outside, stand close to the wall and face the carved portal, tilting up to catch it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the outside and general views of the nave. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tomb and its statues in one frame, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for single statues and the carved panels.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap a bright part of the bronze and slide it a little darker so the statues keep their detail.
card.best_time: Outside looks best in soft daylight, like morning or late afternoon, which also tends to mean fewer people in your way. It can be dim inside at any time of day, so pick whatever suits your visit and let night mode do its thing.
card.selfie_here: Try the courtyard of the Hofburg next door, where the church can share the frame with you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the church over your shoulder, and check it looks right when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Universitätsstraße from the church front while you stand by the church, so the whole facade fits in with the mountains behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules inside can differ from outside, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Pick your favourite bronze figure, get close and take a portrait of it, then try to strike the same pose in a quick selfie.
card.good_to_know: Emperor Ferdinand I built the Court Church in 1553 as a memorial to his grandfather, Emperor Maximilian I. Maximilian isn't actually buried here, which is why the tomb is a cenotaph. The church also holds the tomb of Andreas Hofer, Tyrol's national hero, and a Renaissance organ from 1560.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Court Church (Hofkirche) at Universitätsstraße 2, next to the Hofburg, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Outside, stand close to the wall and face the carved portal, tilting up to catch it.

card.hook: Alpenzoo is a zoo that climbs a mountain, and the paths wind uphill so every bend gives you a new angle. Bears and wolves get the fame, but the snail-shaped pavilion might steal your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Head into Alpenzoo: it's about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the zoo, heading south-east. Stop where the zoo is spread out in front of you and face the wooded slope and the paths running across it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for enclosures and paths. Switch to zoom 0.5x for the slope, the snail-shaped pavilion and views through the trees. For animals further back, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) so you don't have to lean over any barriers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the animal or the snail pavilion on one of the crossing points, leaving some trees or path around it to show the hillside.
card.best_time: Pick a bright but not harsh day, when the shade under the trees is soft and the animals are more likely to be up and about. Check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Go to the viewing platform of the Fox, Badger and Friends Shelter, inside the central building a few metres below ground level. It's at the zoo's highest point, so use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and put the open Inn Valley view behind you, with no enclosures in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Some paths are quite steep, so allow time and watch your footing while you hold your phone.
card.challenge: Find the snail-shaped pavilion and frame it on a grid crossing point with trees around it. Bonus points if it looks like it's sneaking through the woods.
card.good_to_know: Alpenzoo was founded on 22 September 1962 by the zoologist Hans Psenner, and it's one of the highest-elevation zoos in Europe. It's home to about 2,000 animals from 150 species, and it's the only zoo in the world that shows the wallcreeper. The snail-shaped timber pavilion opened in August 2017.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Alpenzoo: it's about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the zoo, heading south-east. Stop where the zoo is spread out in front of you and face the wooded slope and the paths running across it.

card.hook: Here's a twist: at St. Anne's Column, the column isn't the star of this shot. The real picture is the painted Baroque facades with the mountains rising right behind the rooftops.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Maria-Theresien-Straße and Meraner Straße, on the building corner at the Meraner Straße intersection, a short walk from the column. Face the colourful facades at the junction so the mountains sit above the rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facades and the mountains above them. Go to 0.5x to fit the whole junction in, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out rooftop and facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a facade edge up with a vertical grid line so the buildings don't lean, then keep the rooftops in the lower half and give the mountains the top.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on this busy street. If you're facing north around midday, the sun tends to be behind you and lights up the fronts of the buildings and the column.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrian street just south of the column, on the south side of St. Anne's Column. Use the front camera (try 0.5x) and turn so the column and the Nordkette mountains are behind you, and check the framing on screen before you commit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the south end of the street near the Triumphal Arch (Triumphpforte) and look north, while you pose in front of the column so it sits centre-frame with the Nordkette rising behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is busy, so be patient and keep clear of the café seating. Please don't sit on the monument's steps, as café owners dislike it. The street is sometimes used for events, so check the official site first if you're planning around a particular date.
card.challenge: Walk up to the column and find all four saints around the base: Anne to the north, Cassian to the west, Vigilius to the east and George to the south. Then get a photo of each.
card.good_to_know: The column was put up to give thanks after the last Bavarian troops were driven out of the Tyrol on Saint Anne's Day (26 July) in 1703, and it was consecrated in 1706. It's red Kramsach marble, designed by the sculptor Cristoforo Benedetti, and rises 13 metres. On top stands the Virgin as the Woman of the Apocalypse.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Maria-Theresien-Straße and Meraner Straße, on the building corner at the Meraner Straße intersection, a short walk from the column. Face the colourful facades at the junction so the mountains sit above the rooftops.

card.hook: Trams, buses and cars swirl around a big stone arch, and it still manages to look calm. That's the Triumphal Arch, and its solid, symmetrical shape makes it a very easy thing to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, right at the Triumphal Arch at the southern end of Maria-Theresien-Straße. There's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the arch and try to get the whole thing in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the arch with the buildings around it. If traffic or railings stop you stepping back, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the carved reliefs and any distant mountains.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arch, then slide the brightness a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, when mountains are most likely to show behind the arch. Earlier or later in the day usually means fewer people and vehicles in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the pedestrian boulevard on Maria-Theresien-Straße just north of the arch, where the arch closes off the end of the street as your backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the arch over your shoulder. It's not a set selfie spot, so check how it looks on the day.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the little traffic island in the middle of the road at the roundabout, only if it's safe, so they can fit you, the whole arch, the mountains and the old buildings into one shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The arch sits at a busy junction with cars, buses and trams, in a roundabout. Watch the traffic and never step into the road for a better angle.
card.challenge: Frame the view through the central opening and see which mountain fills the gap. It might be the Serles, but check on the day.
card.good_to_know: The arch was built in 1765 for the wedding of Archduke Leopold, son of Empress Maria Theresa, to the Spanish princess Maria Luisa. Leopold's father, Francis Stephen, died unexpectedly soon after, so the south side shows the wedding and the north side remembers the emperor. Unusually for an arch like this, it's made of stone rather than wood, reusing blocks from the old outer city gate.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon, right at the Triumphal Arch at the southern end of Maria-Theresien-Straße. There's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the arch and try to get the whole thing in one frame.

selfie_spots.why: Guides describe the arch at the end of this street as an excellent last backdrop for photos, and the boulevard leads straight toward the Nordkette.

card.hook: Look for two towers and a big dome poking up through a sea of green copper roofs. That's Innsbruck Cathedral, and in the Old Town it's hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Stand on Domplatz, the square in front of the cathedral, and face the curved west façade. It's the easiest spot to fit the whole front and both towers into one clean shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the façade. If the towers won't fit, tap 0.5x. For the saints in their niches, try zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean, then tap the bright stonework and drag the slider a touch darker to keep the pale façade's detail.
card.best_time: Go when the sun is low and warm. It brings out the carved detail in the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Domplatz facing the west front, so the twin towers sit behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, to squeeze in more of the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across Domplatz from the façade, far enough that the whole front and both towers fit, while you stand in the foreground with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Taking photos inside costs a small fee of €1, paid in cash at a machine near the entrance. Keep the printed ticket in case staff ask to see it, and follow any signs posted on site.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide with both towers dead straight on the gridlines, and one close-up of your favourite stone saint. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The present church went up between 1717 and 1724 on the site of a twelfth-century Romanesque church. It was badly damaged in an air raid in December 1944 and restored between 1946 and 1950. The limestone saints in the façade niches were made between 1941 and 1960, and the church became a cathedral in 1964.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Domplatz, the square in front of the cathedral, and face the curved west façade. It's the easiest spot to fit the whole front and both towers into one clean shot.

card.hook: Picture a huge white roof that looks like a wave frozen mid-swoosh, with mountain slopes piled up right behind it. That's the Hungerburg station, and it's the reason this ride is worth a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Hermann-Buhl-Platz, the square right in front of the Hungerburg top station, and face the station. You want the white canopy in the foreground and the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole canopy and the slopes into one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes above the roof.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright white canopy, then slide it a touch darker so the concrete keeps its detail instead of turning plain white.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light on the white concrete is kinder than the harsher glare of the afternoon. In winter, snow can blow into the top station and sometimes causes partial closures, so leave yourself some wiggle room.
card.selfie_here: Head to the free viewing platform just outside the Hungerburg station. Stand on the terrace with the station behind you and the city view in front, and use the front camera. If you want more of that curvy canopy in the shot, try 0.5x and hold the phone a little higher.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the viewing terrace outside the station, facing it, so the curved canopy fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The funicular and its stations are part of the public transport system and may be ticketed or partly closed in snow, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch down a little and make the roof sweep even more dramatic, then see if you can keep the canopy a clean, simple shape with no stray people at the edges.
card.good_to_know: Zaha Hadid designed the stations. The current line opened on 1 December 2007 and replaced an older railway that ran from 1906 to 2005. The line climbs 288 m and crosses the Inn on a 242 m S-shaped cable-stayed bridge. The two cars have silver frames, with a yellow compartment on one and a blue one on the other.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Hermann-Buhl-Platz, the square right in front of the Hungerburg top station, and face the station. You want the white canopy in the foreground and the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes rising behind it.

card.hook: Giant chess boards, a pavilion from 1733 and a lawn you're not allowed to walk on: the Hofgarten is a very polite place to take photos. Stick to the paths and it rewards you with trees, ponds and plenty of variety.
card.stand_here: Stand about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You're in the Hofgarten, right beside the Old Town.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the wide lawns and trees. Switch to 1x for the pavilion and ponds, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details and for the chess players, from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the pavilion or a pond on a lower line, with a tree trunk or branch at the edge of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is worth a try for softer light under the trees, and a still day might give you a pond reflection. If you'd like fewer people in the shot, a weekday morning is your best bet.
card.selfie_here: Go to the pond in the centre of the garden, turn your back to the pavilion and use the front camera. Its big open windows make a nice portrait backdrop. For mountains instead, try the garden's north edge, with the Nordkette framed by tree branches behind you (it's an approximate spot, so look around).
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pond side and shoot toward the pavilion, while you stand so the pavilion fills the background behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the paths, because walking on the ornate lawns isn't permitted. Only the sunbathing lawn by the children's playpark is meant for use. Check the official site for current access and palm house visiting times.
card.challenge: Take one wide frame of the whole scene, then get three close-ups: the pavilion, a pond edge and the trunk of the oldest tree you can find.
card.good_to_know: The Hofgarten is a protected 10-hectare park that began in the sixteenth century under Archduke Ferdinand II. It has been a Renaissance garden, a French formal garden and, since 1858, an English landscape garden. Some plants were reportedly planted by Empress Maria Theresa herself, so look for the older trees.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You're in the Hofgarten, right beside the Old Town.

card.hook: Picture a wedding cake that someone turned into a house. That's Helbling House: bows, shells, masks and little sculptures piled over every inch of the front, and it's right across from the Golden Roof.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße in Innsbruck's Old Town, in the street directly opposite the house. Face the façade with the Golden Roof beside it, and the whole front fits in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the full façade with the Golden Roof next to it. If the street is too tight, tap 0.5x. For the stucco angels and masks, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the house's straight edges up with them so the building doesn't lean, then tap the façade and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the stucco keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go when the light falls across the front, because the raised stucco throws little shadows and looks properly 3D. Bright, even daylight works too, and early morning is likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the square in front of the Golden Roof and face the Golden Roof, so the Helbling House façade is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more of the frills in, and hold the phone a bit low so the house rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand directly across the street from the façade while you stand in front of the house, so you and the whole building, with the Golden Roof beside it, fit in one shot.
card.challenge: Step up close, fill the frame with the stucco, and see how many masks and angels you can find in one photo.
card.good_to_know: The house began in the fifteenth century as townhouses with an early Gothic look. The frothy Rococo stucco you see today was finished in 1732 by Anton Gigl. It's named after Sebastian Helbling, who owned it from 1800 to 1827. You can only look at it from outside, so all the fun happens from the street.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße in Innsbruck's Old Town, in the street directly opposite the house. Face the façade with the Golden Roof beside it, and the whole front fits in one frame.

card.hook: The big star here is a painting of about 1,000 square metres, but it's tucked inside, so your outdoor photo has to do the bragging. Luckily, the museum sits on its own big site at Bergisel with plenty of sky around it.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon, which sits in the middle of the museum's outline, then walk back outside to a good distance from the entrance. Turn around and face the building so you can fit much of it in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole building. If it won't fit, switch to 0.5x, but only then, because it can stretch the edges. For the entrance or a sign, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building, and fewer people too. Check the museum's website for its current opening times.
card.selfie_here: Head to the panorama pavilion terrace next to the Kaiserjäger Museum, behind the Kaiserjägermuseum building. Use the front camera (0.5x if you want more in), and check that the museum is behind your shoulder, with the Innsbruck and Nordkette views around you.
card.ask_someone: If someone is up on the Bergisel bridge (Bergisel-Brücke), ask them to take a photo of the museum while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, ask staff about photography rules when you arrive. Outside, stick to the public areas.
card.challenge: Take three frames: one wide with lots of sky, one close on the entrance, and one with a tiny you in it for scale.
card.good_to_know: The Giant Panorama Painting shows the Tyrolean Rebellion of 1809. It moved here in September 2010, and the museum opened on 12 March 2011. An underground link joins it to the Kaiserjäger Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon, which sits in the middle of the museum's outline, then walk back outside to a good distance from the entrance. Turn around and face the building so you can fit much of it in.
